name: Chechnya
summary_text: Chechnya is an autonomous republic of Russia, and visitors there stand under the federal framework that governs the country. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents took effect; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advises against all travel to Russia at Level 4, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.  Chechnya's security services operate against LGBT people with a severity not documented elsewhere in Russia. Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017) established that a police purge began in February 2017: men believed to be gay were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. Some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families barely alive from beatings, with captors outing them to relatives and urging honour killings. The investigation found that top regional officials knew of the operation, despite the regional leader's public denial.  The purge was not a single episode. Novaya Gazeta (11 January 2019) reported renewed persecution of gay men in the republic, with warnings circulated through the administrators of LGBT groups on the VKontakte social network telling those still at large to leave; the regional leader's press secretary denied the reports. That reporting followed the paper's April 2017 investigation into the torture and killing of gay men, for which no criminal case was ever opened.  Detention has since been converted into coercion toward the war in Ukraine. The Insider (4 September 2024) reported that the monitoring group SK SOS documented Chechen security forces pressuring detained gay men into military service: at least seven were sent to the frontlines and at least one was already killed, and the methods predate the mobilisation order of 21 September 2022. In early September 2022, six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned that they would be sent to the front.  The same machinery operates on the wider population. An investigation by the Memorial Human Rights Centre, reported by OC Media, found a mass wave of unlawful detentions in which people were taken in over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, held at police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, and forced to sign service contracts; in some cases a family had to produce two "volunteers" before a detained relative would be released.  The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024, involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing. It assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and notes that the 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation exposes support for it to 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising to 6 to 10 years, with violence spreading beyond the region.

name: Dagestan
summary_text: Dagestan stands under the national framework of Russia, where the risks facing transgender visitors have sharpened markedly since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and the United States State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The same statutes operate inside Dagestan as they do in every other Russian region.  The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) names the North Caucasus, including Dagestan, as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North Caucasus authorities from 2017 to 2024 involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing, and it assesses transgender people and visible advocates as a specific category within that finding rather than treating the region's risk as applying only to sexual orientation.  Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia and separately warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, singling out the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan. The same advisory states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of Interior, a requirement that applies to visitors as well as residents and that can be refused without stated grounds.  David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. For a transgender visitor this means the exposure is not limited to public expression: being recognised as trans in a domestic setting carries the same risk.

sources.title: European Court of Human Rights - 2010 ruling on pride parade bans

sources.detail: Cited in text as: 'In 2010, the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating against the LGBTQ community, after local governments systemically refused to issue permits to pride parades' and Alexeyev / Moscow Pride case
